messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Aroha's Burden

Aroha was twenty years old when her husband Marcus first hit her. She had been married for fourteen months—a union her Samoan family had celebrated with a fiafia, though her mother had harboured quiet doubts. That first night, two weeks before she came to the intake appointment, Marcus had been drinking. She had asked him about his spending, about the credit card statement she'd found. His hand moved faster than her mind could register. She fell against the kitchen counter. The pain was shocking, but what stayed with her was the sound—the wet crack of her lip splitting—and the way his face had transformed into something she didn't recognize, something that made her certain, in that moment, that she was going to die.

He apologized immediately. He cried. He said it would never happen again. Aroha believed him because she needed to, because the alternative—that the man she had married was capable of this—felt like her own failure of judgment, her own stupidity. She had chosen him. She had stood in front of her family and promised. Over the following days, as the swelling faded to bruises she covered with foundation, she found herself replaying every moment leading up to that night. What had she said that was wrong? How had she provoked him? The questions spiralled endlessly, and she couldn't stop asking them, even though each answer only deepened her shame.

The incident itself was brief—perhaps thirty seconds of violence—but it had fractured something fundamental in how Aroha moved through the world. Loud noises now sent her heart racing. A car door slamming in the parking lot outside her design studio made her flinch so violently that her colleague Jade had asked if she was all right. She wasn't. The sound had transported her back to the kitchen, to the moment before impact, to the terror of not knowing what was coming. Worse was being alone with men. She had scheduled a client meeting with a prospective male contractor, and within five minutes of sitting across from him in the consultation room, her chest had tightened so severely she'd had to excuse herself. She'd told him she was unwell. The truth was that being in a closed space with a man—any man—made her body scream that danger was imminent.

Seeing Marcus was the worst trigger of all. He had come to pick up some belongings from their apartment three days ago, and she had locked herself in the bedroom until he left. Her body had remained rigid for hours afterward, adrenaline flooding her system with no outlet. She had checked the locks on the windows repeatedly. She had looked behind her as she moved through the apartment, certain he might return.

To manage the fear, Aroha had begun avoiding circumstances that reminded her of the event. She no longer went into the kitchen after dark. She had stopped going out alone. She refused to be in any room by herself if there was a possibility someone might enter—she kept her apartment door open, or she stayed in the living room where she could see the entrance. This meant she had essentially stopped working from home, though her job as an interior designer increasingly required it. She was falling behind on a residential project. Her boss had begun to notice. She hadn't told anyone at the office what had happened.

The rumination was relentless. Lying in bed at night, her body perpetually tense, muscles coiled as though ready to fight or flee, Aroha replayed the incident obsessively. She blamed herself. If she hadn't asked about the credit card, if she had been more careful with money, if she had simply stayed quiet. Sometimes she felt the full force of that night's terror—the panic, the helplessness—without any clear image attached to it, just the raw emotional intensity crashing through her body as though it were happening again.

What frightened her most was the certainty that had crystallized in the aftermath: people couldn't be trusted. Her husband had hidden his capacity for violence. Her family would judge her if they knew. The world felt fundamentally unsafe, and she had come to believe that her life as she had known it was destroyed, that she no longer belonged anywhere—not in her marriage, not in her own home, not even in her own body. When she finally called the clinic, it was because she couldn't function anymore, and because some small part of her wondered if there was any way back from this.
